summary: The only stone fire lookout left in Oregon, built 1932 near Molalla, unstaffed since the early 1960s, restored by volunteers starting 1991, and open to the public to visit and stay overnight free.

facts.status_note: Not staffed since the early 1960s; restored and open to public visitation/overnight stays

access.note: Open to the public for day use and overnight stays, first-come first-served, no permit; reached via a long hike from Rooster Rock Trailhead on the Table Rock Trail, or a steep closed fire road from South Molalla River Road

visit.trail_note: Long, difficult hike from Rooster Rock Trailhead (Table Rock Wilderness) or steep closed fire road from South Molalla River Road; good map/orientation skills recommended

facts.agency: Bureau of Land Management (formerly Oregon Department of Forestry)

events.note: Fire detection site established with only a primitive rangefinder, no cabin yet
Stone-and-wood cupola cabin built by John Oblack and an unnamed Portland stonemason, using native stone
Sand Mountain Society states the lookout was staffed until 1963, under Oregon Department of Forestry management
BLM states it was determined in 1964 that Pechuck was no longer needed for fire suppression, due to aerial patrols and better roads
Listed on the National Historic Lookout Register, August 18, 1990, the second site registered
Volunteer-led re-roofing project begins, organized by Jim Borders with the Molalla community and Sand Mountain Society members Doug Newman, Don Allen, and Bill Joy
Added to the World Fire Lookout Register
firelookout.com states the lookout was restored in 1995 (a separate or later restoration effort than the 1991 re-roofing)

evidence.supports: 1918 establishment with only a rangefinder; 1932 cabin construction by John Oblack; 1964 determination lookout no longer needed; public access and trail routes
evidence.quote: Originally, the lookout consisted only of a primitive fire detection rangefinder; and some years later, in the early 1930s, a small stone and wood cabin was built. The Pechuck Lookout, also known as a cupola, was built by John Oblack, a Czechoslovakian from Molalla with help from an unknown stone mason from Portland.
in 1964, it was determined that Pechuck was no longer needed as part of a fire suppression system
The Pechuck Lookout is open to the public for visitation and overnight use on a first-come, first-served basis.

evidence.supports: Access route via Rooster Rock Trailhead or closed fire road
evidence.quote: The most scenic route to the lookout is from the Rooster Rock Trailhead on the southeast corner of the Table Rock Wilderness... It is also possible to walk up the long, steep, closed fire road from South Molalla River Road.

evidence.supports: NHLR 1990 and World Fire Lookout Register 1992 listing
evidence.quote: Pechuck Lookout was ultimately placed on the National Historic Lookout Register in 1990 and the World Fire Lookout Register in 1992.

evidence.supports: Built 1932, locally quarried stone, staffed until 1963 under ODF
evidence.quote: Year Built 1932... Style Unique with locally quarried stone... The lookout was staffed until 1963 and managed by Oregon Department

evidence.supports: 1991 restoration effort led by Jim Borders and Sand Mountain Society members, later Friends of Pechuck
evidence.quote: In 1991, Doug Newman arranged for Don Allen and Bill Joy to meet up with some local folks from the Molalla area, led by Jim Borders, and help them kick off the restoration of Pechuck Lookout... the project was ultimately adopted by a separate group called Friends of Pechuck

evidence.supports: Second lookout listed on the register
evidence.quote: Pechuck Lookout was strategically honored as only the second lookout listed on the Historic Fire Lookout Register.

evidence.supports: Stone cupola resembling Timberline Lodge, survived because razing was too costly, restored by volunteers led by Pete Bond
evidence.quote: The structure is a cupola and is especially unique in that it was built of stone reminiscent of nearby Timberline Lodge on Mount Hood. Although not in use for many years, the building undoubtedly escaped razing because of the effort that would have been required to remove it. The building has been rerooted and restored by a group of volunteers led by Pete Bond, Trails Coordinator for the Oregon Department of State Parks in Salem.

evidence.supports: Established 1918, cupola built 1932, not staffed since 1960s, restored 1995
evidence.quote: Established with a cabin in 1918, this stone and frame cupola cabin, built in 1932, has not been staffed since the 1960's. Restored in 1995, it is listed on the National Historic Lookout Register.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sand Mountain Society says staffed until 1963; BLM says the 'no longer needed' determination came in 1964. These likely describe the same transition from different angles (last staffed season vs. formal decision) rather than a true conflict, so the story reports both without picking one.

NHLR credits a restoration led by Pete Bond of Oregon State Parks; Sand Mountain Society describes an earlier 1991 re-roofing led by Jim Borders and Molalla-area volunteers with SMS help, later passed to 'Friends of Pechuck'; firelookout.com cites a 1995 restoration. These may represent sequential restoration phases by different groups rather than contradicting each other; the story presents the 1991 effort as documented by SMS and flags that other restoration work (per NHLR and firelookout.com) also occurred.

notes_for_editor: Minor unresolved discrepancy on exactly which restoration campaign (1991 SMS/Jim Borders re-roofing, a Pete Bond-led Oregon State Parks restoration per NHLR, or a 1995 date per firelookout.com) is the 'main' one; these may all be real, sequential volunteer efforts. Current brief listed access as 'public' which matches what we found; staffing/status fields can be added since the brief omitted them. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the story described John Oblack as a 'Czech stonemason's helper,' which isn't in any source (source 1/BLM calls him 'a Czechoslovakian from Molalla with help from an unknown stone mason from Portland,' i.e. Oblack built it himself with an unnamed mason's help, not the other way around); corrected to match the source wording. Spot-checked the 1918 rangefinder-only origin and the 'four sides / 360-degree view' claim directly against the BLM page, and the 1991 'autumn rains' re-roofing detail directly against the Sand Mountain Society page; all three confirmed. The 'only stone lookout remaining in Oregon' claim was also confirmed on the BLM page (not previously quoted in the evidence list, but present in the source).
